rationale: The book's core definition unifies every cited use (ritual status without guilt, moral defilement, vessels, foods, and NT cleansing) under a single functional idea—removal of whatever bars permitted contact/approach/use—while preserving the explicit biblical distinctions (holy/common vs. clean/unclean; cleanse vs. sanctify). The common moral-spiritual reading must either ignore non-sin uncleanness texts or treat them as secondary types, creating more exceptions and collapsing categories Scripture keeps separate. No supplied text requires equating uncleanness with guilt or collapsing cleanse into sanctify; the book's distinctions therefore explain the full evidence with fewer unsupported steps.
book_core_identification: To cleanse is to remove the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean describes what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and does not always mean guilt.
book_secondary_elaborations: Cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit; sanctification then places the cleansed vessel under a holy claim and appointed use
The three operations (wash/cleanse, sanctify, justify) answer three distinct questions and are not synonyms
Moral applications of clean/unclean vocabulary retain the same functional shape without erasing the non-moral cases
strongest_counter_interpretation: Clean/unclean is primarily ritual-purity language that symbolizes moral and spiritual condition before God (uncleanness = sin/defilement/unfitness for holy presence; cleanness = holiness/moral purity); cleansing therefore primarily means forgiveness of sin and sanctification accomplished through Christ's blood, with OT rites as types of that spiritual cleansing.
counter_core_identification: Uncleanness represents sin/defilement making one unfit for God; cleansing represents forgiveness and sanctification by Christ.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the governing sense is fitness for contact/approach/use that can exist without guilt, and treats non-sin uncleanness (childbirth, marital relations, corpse contact) as either peripheral or merely typological of moral guilt rather than genuine instances of the same category.
counter_case: Psalms 51:2, 10; Isaiah 1:16-18; 1 John 1:7, 9 and Hebrews 9-10 explicitly link cleansing language to sin and Christ's blood
Mark 7 / Matthew 15 relocate defilement from external food/ritual to the heart, supporting a moral-spiritual primary sense
Traditional Christian reading consistently treats OT purity rites as foreshadowing NT forgiveness and sanctification
Acts 10 and related texts show clean/unclean categories being re-applied to moral/spiritual and ethnic barriers
book_explanatory_advantages: Directly accounts for Leviticus 12:2; 15:18; Numbers 19:11 where uncleanness occurs without any charge of sin or guilt
Preserves the two distinctions commanded in Leviticus 10:10 and rebuked as erased in Ezekiel 22:26 (holy/common vs. clean/unclean)
Explains why Paul can list washed, sanctified, and justified as three distinct operations in 1 Corinthians 6:11 and why Ephesians 5:26 can say 'sanctify and cleanse'
Applies uniformly to physical objects, food, bodies, and moral cases without redefining the word mid-stream or importing untested synonyms
counter_explanatory_advantages: Matches the dominant pastoral and systematic-theology usage of the terms for sin and forgiveness
Readily integrates the major NT cleansing texts that speak of blood, word, and conscience
Provides a single redemptive-historical storyline from OT type to Christ
decisive_sources: Leviticus 10:10 (explicit distinction of holy/unholy and unclean/clean)
Ephesians 5:26 (sanctify and cleanse as coordinated but non-identical actions)
Psalm 51:2, 10; 1 John 1:7, 9 (moral extension of the same functional vocabulary)
unresolved_objections: Some readers may still prefer to treat the non-moral cases as merely preparatory types rather than full instances of the category
The precise boundary between ceremonial and moral defilement in mixed texts remains debated in scholarship
